title: SSL pinning in a mobile app
tagline: Pin the server's key, so a proxy holding a trusted certificate still reads nothing.
intro: TLS proves the certificate is signed by a trusted CA. Pinning adds a second question: is it the key we expect?

sections.title: What it does
sections.summary: One extra check, after the normal one passes.

blocks.caption: The pin check runs after the chain is already valid.

items.label: App connects
items.detail: The app opens a TLS connection. Nothing has been trusted yet
explain: TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the S in HTTPS: a handshake that agrees on keys first, then encrypts everything after it. TLS 1.3 is the version in use today.
At this instant the app holds one hostname, api.example.com, and an open socket. It has no idea whether the machine answering is your server or a laptop in the same café.
Concretely: URLSession or OkHttp calls connect(), the TCP three-way handshake finishes, and the first TLS message is about to be written.
Pinning is not a different protocol. It is one extra comparison the app runs later, after everything the OS normally checks has already passed.

items.label: Server sends its chain
items.detail: The leaf certificate for the domain, plus the intermediates linking it up to a root
explain: A certificate is three things: a public key, a name, and a signature from whoever vouches for the pair. None of it is secret — it is designed to be handed to strangers.
Call your server's one cert_A. It holds pub_key_A, the public half of a key pair whose private half, priv_key_A, never leaves your server.
The chain is cert_A signed by an intermediate (say R3), and R3 signed by a root CA (say ISRG Root X1) that shipped inside the phone years ago.
Chains exist so the root's private key can stay offline in a vault: it signs a handful of intermediates, and those intermediates sign millions of leaf certificates.
Anyone can send a chain. The proxy in the next section sends cert_X holding pub_key_X, chained to a CA it talked you into installing — same structure, different key.

items.label: OS validates the chain
items.detail: The device checks the signatures up to a CA in its own trust store, and the dates
explain: Check one, signatures: cert_A must verify against R3's public key, and R3 against a root already in the device's trust store. Break the chain anywhere and it fails.
Check two, the name: the hostname you dialled must appear in cert_A's SAN list (Subject Alternative Name), the modern replacement for the old CN field.
Check three, the dates: notBefore ≤ now ≤ notAfter, measured against the device clock — which is why a phone set to 2019 fails every HTTPS request at once.
A trust store is just a list of root certificates. iOS ships around 150 of them, and a profile you install adds one more with exactly the same authority.
That is the hole the next section walks through: an attacker's CA sits in that list by your own consent, so cert_X passes all three checks. Nothing is broken — it is working as designed.

items.label: App compares the pin
items.detail: Only now: hash the public key out of that certificate and look for it in the app's list
explain: SPKI (SubjectPublicKeyInfo) is the field inside a certificate holding the public key together with its algorithm: 'this is an RSA-2048 key, and here are its bytes'.
The app takes SPKI(pub_key_A), hashes it with SHA-256, base64-encodes the 32 bytes, and ends up with a 44-character string — call it pin_A, written sha256/AAAA1111…=.
pin_A was compiled into the app at build time. The comparison itself is ordinary string equality; nothing clever happens at this step.
Pinning the key rather than the certificate is what survives renewal: reissue cert_A as cert_A2 with the same key pair and pin_A does not change by one character.

items.label: Match → continue
items.detail: The peer holds the exact key you shipped, so the request finally goes out
explain: A match means SHA-256(SPKI) of the certificate that just arrived equals pin_A, so the peer is presenting pub_key_A.
Earlier in the handshake, CertificateVerify proved the peer also holds priv_key_A. Copying cert_A off a public website gets an attacker nothing without that private half.
Together the two say: this is the machine holding your key, not merely a machine holding a certificate some CA was willing to sign.
Only now is application data written to the socket — the Authorization header, the cookies, the request body.

items.label: Mismatch → abort
items.detail: Valid certificate, wrong key — the connection closes before any data is sent
explain: A mismatch means the hash of the key that arrived, pin_X, is in no entry of the app's pin list, however impeccable the chain around it looked.
The client sends a TLS alert and closes the socket. iOS surfaces NSURLErrorServerCertificateUntrusted (-1202); OkHttp throws SSLPeerUnverifiedException with the offending pin printed.
Nothing left the device: the abort happens before the first byte of the HTTP request, so no token, cookie or body was ever exposed.
Log the pin that was presented. A rotation you got wrong looks identical to an attack from the outside, and that log line is the only thing that tells them apart.

items: Stops a proxy whose CA was installed on the device — Charles, mitmproxy, an MDM profile.
Stops a compromised or mis-issuing CA signing a certificate for your domain.
Does not stop a rooted device: Frida can patch the check out.
Raises the cost of intercepting traffic. It is not a wall.

sections.title: Scenario: a fake Wi-Fi
sections.summary: What a coffee-shop network can do to an app that trusts the device.

blocks.caption: The same network, with and without a pin.

items.label: Free_Airport_WiFi
items.detail: A network named to look ordinary, run by someone who wants your traffic
explain: An access point is a name (the SSID) plus a DHCP server. A laptop with internet sharing on, or a cheap travel router, is both of those in two minutes.
Whoever runs it also runs DNS: the phone asks 'where is api.example.com?' and believes the answer, say 192.168.4.2 — the attacker's own machine.
Phones re-join networks whose name they have seen before, so an SSID copied from a chain of cafés is joined with nobody tapping anything at all.
None of this is exotic; it is the standard first lab in a security course. Proxyman in the next section is the same setup with your own consent.

items.label: A portal asks to install a profile
items.detail: The page looks like a normal login step, but installing it adds the attacker's CA
explain: A captive portal is the page a network shows before it lets you out to the internet, and everyone has been trained to tap through whatever it asks.
What downloads is a .mobileconfig: a signed bundle of settings that can add a root CA — call it Airport_CA — to the device's trust store.
iOS wants two steps: install it under Settings → Profile Downloaded, then switch it on under General → About → Certificate Trust Settings. Two taps each.
From that moment, whoever holds Airport_CA's private key can sign a certificate for any hostname in the world and this phone will accept it.

items.label: The app calls api.example.com
items.detail: The proxy answers instead of your server, holding a certificate it issued itself
explain: DNS is answered by the attacker, so the connection lands on their proxy — mitmproxy, Burp or Proxyman: a program that speaks TLS on both sides at once.
SNI (Server Name Indication) is the hostname the client sends in the clear inside ClientHello, so that one IP address can host many sites. It is also what tells the proxy which name to forge.
The proxy reads api.example.com from SNI, generates cert_X for that exact name on the spot, signs it with Airport_CA, and presents it holding pub_key_X.
It also opens its own connection onward to the real api.example.com, so replies are genuine and the app keeps working. Nothing looks wrong to the person holding the phone.

items.label: The chain looks valid
items.detail: Every normal check passes, because the device was just told to trust that CA
explain: cert_X is signed by Airport_CA, and Airport_CA is in the trust store because you put it there. Signature check: passes.
cert_X's SAN list says api.example.com, because the proxy copied the name straight out of SNI. Hostname check: passes.
cert_X was issued seconds ago and is valid for a year. Date check: passes.
All three OS checks pass and the padlock is drawn. This is precisely why 'HTTPS with a padlock' and 'talking to your server' are two different statements.

items.label: No pin → readable
items.detail: The proxy reads and rewrites everything: tokens, request bodies, responses
explain: The proxy holds priv_key_X, so it decrypts everything the app sends: Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi…, the JSON body, the cookies, all of it.
It can rewrite as easily as read — change a price, flip isPremium to true, delay or drop a response — and the app cannot tell, because the bytes arrive over a perfectly valid TLS session.
Refresh tokens are the real prize. An access token expires in an hour; a refresh token keeps someone inside the account for weeks.
This is the same tooling you use to debug your own app. The only difference between that and this is who installed the CA, and whether you agreed to it.

items.label: Pin → dropped
items.detail: The key in that certificate is not the one built into the app, so nothing is sent
explain: The app computes SHA-256(SPKI(pub_key_X)) = pin_X and compares it with its list, which contains only pin_A. Not equal, so the handshake is aborted.
It makes no difference that Airport_CA is trusted: pinning skips the question 'who signed this?' entirely and asks 'is this my key?'.
The abort lands before any request is written, so the attacker is left with a TLS alert and nothing else — no token, no headers, no body.
That is the whole value of pinning, and it comes down to comparing two 44-character strings.

items: The session token in the Authorization header, replayable from anywhere.
Every request body: credentials at login, personal data after it.
The responses too — a balance, a price or a feature flag rewritten before the app sees it.
Nothing looks wrong to the user: the padlock is there and the certificate is valid.

body: The device is not compromised and the user did nothing careless. Trusting one extra CA is enough, and a captive portal is a normal-looking place to be asked.

sections.title: How Proxyman intercepts a simulator
sections.summary: The same interception as above, on an iOS Simulator, run by you.

body: On a simulator, Proxyman has to be trusted twice: once in the Mac's keychain and once inside the simulator's own trust store. Watching where those two installs land is the shortest explanation of what pinning takes away.

blocks.caption: Two certificate installs, and the two ways it ends.

items.label: Proxyman CA → the Mac's keychain
items.detail: The root is added to the keychain and marked Always Trust, or nothing on the Mac believes a word of it
explain: On first run Proxyman generates its own root CA — call it Proxyman_CA — and keeps the private key on this Mac. Every certificate you are about to see forged is signed with it.
Installing puts the root into the keychain; trusting it is the separate step of setting 'When using this certificate: Always Trust' in Keychain Access.
macOS asks for your password because a trusted root is a system-wide change: Safari, curl and every other Mac app now accept anything Proxyman_CA signs.
This is exactly the step Airport_CA needed in the section above. Same mechanism, same power — the only difference is that you generated this CA yourself.
To see what you just trusted: security find-certificate -c Proxyman -p | openssl x509 -noout -subject -fingerprint.

items.label: The same CA → each simulator
items.detail: Certificate → Install Certificate on iOS Simulators writes the root into every simulator's own trust store
explain: A simulator is a separate iOS system with its own keychain, stored under ~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/Devices/<UDID>/. It never reads the Mac's keychain.
The menu item runs xcrun simctl keychain <udid> add-root-cert proxyman-ca.pem for each simulator you tick — the same command you can run by hand in a script.
Do it per device: an iPhone 16 and an iPhone SE are two simulators with two trust stores, and one you create tomorrow starts empty again.
Relaunch the app afterwards. A running process keeps the trust it evaluated at launch, so the reliable move is to reboot the simulator entirely.
Erase All Content and Settings throws the store away with everything else, which is the usual reason an interception that worked last week 'suddenly stopped'.

items.label: The app calls api.example.com
items.detail: The simulator shares the Mac's network stack, so there is no Wi-Fi proxy to set on a phone
explain: The simulator is a process on your Mac rather than a virtual machine with its own network card, so it uses the Mac's network stack directly.
That means there is no Wi-Fi screen to open and no proxy host and port to type: the settings you would use on a real iPhone simply do not exist here.
Proxyman makes itself the macOS system HTTP/HTTPS proxy while it runs — the same field under Settings → Network → Proxies — and the simulator inherits it.
Concretely: URLSession in the simulator sends CONNECT api.example.com:443 to 127.0.0.1:9090 instead of opening a socket to your server.
On a physical device you would do the other two things instead: set the proxy by hand on that Wi-Fi network, or let Proxyman's VPN mode capture the traffic.

items.label: Proxyman mints a certificate
items.detail: It generates a leaf for that exact hostname on the spot and signs it with the CA both sides now trust
explain: Proxyman reads the hostname from the CONNECT line and from SNI in ClientHello, then generates cert_X for exactly that name, valid from this second.
cert_X is signed by Proxyman_CA and carries pub_key_X — Proxyman's key, not your server's. That one substitution is the whole thing pinning detects.
Both trust stores now accept the signature: the Mac's because you set Always Trust, the simulator's because the root was added to its keychain.
Your app sees a chain of two, cert_X ← Proxyman_CA. The real chain, cert_A ← R3 ← ISRG Root X1, is seen only by Proxyman on the far side.
One certificate is minted per hostname and cached, which is why the first request to a new domain is noticeably slower than the ones after it.

items.label: Two TLS sessions, not one
items.detail: Simulator ↔ Proxyman is decrypted, and Proxyman ↔ server is a second connection Proxyman makes itself
explain: Session one, simulator ↔ Proxyman, is encrypted with keys derived from pub_key_X. Proxyman holds priv_key_X, so it can decrypt every byte.
Session two, Proxyman ↔ api.example.com, is an ordinary TLS connection Proxyman opens itself, validating cert_A the way any client would.
Between the two, the request exists as plaintext in Proxyman's memory — which is precisely the product: a readable, editable, replayable request list.
Your server sees Proxyman as the client. Same request, different TLS session, nothing unusual in the backend logs.
This is the textbook definition of a man in the middle. The honest difference from the café attack is who set it up, and whether the user agreed to it.

items.label: No pin → the request list fills up
items.detail: Headers, tokens, bodies and responses are all readable, which is exactly what makes the tool worth having
explain: You get the whole exchange: GET /v1/profile, Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi…, the JSON body, the response and every header on it.
Breakpoints and Map Local rewrite either direction — return a 500 to test the error path, or force isPremium: true without touching the backend.
It is the same view an attacker gets on a network they control. The tool does not know, and does not care, which of the two you are.
Which is the argument for pinning in one sentence: if your debugging session is this easy to set up, so is theirs.

items.label: Pinned → the handshake fails
items.detail: The forged leaf holds the wrong key, so the app closes the connection before sending any request
explain: The app computes SHA-256(SPKI(pub_key_X)) = pin_X, finds only pin_A in its list, and closes the connection during the handshake.
Proxyman shows the entry in red as a failed TLS handshake, with no body and no headers, because none were ever sent.
Rule of thumb for telling the two failures apart: a certificate you forgot to trust breaks every app on the device, while a pin breaks one app and leaves Safari working.
The way in is a debug build with the check disabled — an #if DEBUG around it, or a debug-only pin holding the hash of Proxyman_CA's key.
Neither may ship. A release build that accepts a debug pin is worse than no pinning at all, because it looks protected and is not.

items: Proxyman → Certificate → Install Certificate on this Mac, then check in Keychain Access that the root really says Always Trust.
Proxyman → Certificate → Install Certificate on iOS Simulators, and tick the simulators you actually run the app on.
Reboot that simulator and launch the app again, so it picks up the trust store it was given rather than the one it started with.
To inspect a pinned app, run a debug build with pinning disabled — never the release build, and never leave the CA trusted afterwards.

body: The simulator keeps that CA until the device is erased, and on the Mac it is trusted by everything you run. Untrust it when you are done debugging, and never install a CA that somebody else generated.

sections.title: What to pin
sections.summary: Three choices, and only one of them survives renewal.

rows: Every renewal, so a few times a year.
Only when the key pair itself changes.
The CA rotates its intermediate, without telling you.
Weak: anyone with a cert from that CA passes.

blocks.caption: Read the SPKI pin off the live server

sections.title: How the app compares the key
sections.summary: Where the pin comes from, and what is actually compared.

blocks.caption: Two sources, reduced the same way, compared as strings.

items.label: Build time
items.detail: You read the key off your own server once, and compile the hash into the app
explain: One command prints it: openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 | openssl x509 -pubkey -noout | openssl pkey -pubin -outform der | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl enc -base64
Run it from a network you trust. A pin read over café Wi-Fi may be the attacker's key, and you would be compiling their key into your app.
The output is pin_A: 44 base64 characters ending in '=', for example sha256/AAAA1111BBBB2222CCCC3333DDDD4444EEEE5555FF=.
Where it goes depends on the platform: NSPinnedDomains in Info.plist on iOS, network_security_config.xml on Android, or a CertificatePinner if you use OkHttp.
A pin is not a secret — it is the hash of a public key. Publishing it costs nothing, which is why the web once sent pins in an HPKP response header.

items.label: Runtime
items.detail: The certificate the peer presented a moment ago, whoever that peer turns out to be
explain: This is whatever the peer presented in this handshake, seconds ago: cert_A from your server, or cert_X from a proxy sitting in the middle.
The app cannot tell which by looking at the chain, because a valid-looking chain is exactly what an attacker with a trusted CA can produce on demand.
So the comparison is against a key, never against a name or an issuer: the key is the one field an attacker cannot usefully copy.
The same code runs in both cases. Only the 44-character string that falls out of it is different.

items.label: SPKI → SHA-256 → base64
items.detail: The key is cut out, hashed and encoded — same steps, so the same key gives the same string
explain: Step one, SPKI: take the SubjectPublicKeyInfo block out of the certificate — the algorithm identifier plus the key bits, in DER encoding.
Step two, SHA-256: hash those bytes down to 32 bytes. The same input always gives the same output, and no other input realistically gives this one.
Step three, base64: turn the 32 bytes into 44 printable characters, so the value can live in a plist, an XML file or a Kotlin string literal.
Why SPKI and not the whole certificate: a certificate changes at every renewal — new dates, new serial number — while the SPKI is identical as long as you keep the key.
Worked example: cert_A holds pub_key_A → SPKI → SHA-256 → sha256/AAAA1111…=. Renew it next year as cert_A2 with the same key pair and the string is unchanged.

items.label: Equal
items.detail: The peer already proved it holds this key during the handshake, so it is your server
explain: Equal means the peer's certificate contains pub_key_A — the public half of a key pair whose private half you generated on your own server.
Together with CertificateVerify, where the server signed the handshake transcript with priv_key_A, this rules out a copied or replayed certificate.
Note what it does not check: whether the CA is reputable, or whether the certificate was issued last week. Those remain the OS's job, and pinning does not replace them.
The code path, concretely: chain valid → hash matches an entry in the list → return true → URLSession resumes → the request finally goes out.

items.label: Different
items.detail: Some other key, no matter who signed it — the connection closes with nothing sent
explain: Different means SHA-256(SPKI) of the presented key matches none of the pins the app holds. Why it differs makes no difference to the outcome.
It covers every case at once: an attacker's CA, a corporate TLS-inspecting proxy, and your own colleague's Proxyman on a debug build.
It also covers your own mistake — a certificate reissued with a fresh key and no release to match. That is the accident the rotation section exists to prevent.
The cost of being wrong here is a failed request; the cost of not checking at all is a stolen refresh token. That trade is what the whole guide is about.

items: Take the certificate the server presented, in DER form.
Cut out the SubjectPublicKeyInfo: the public key plus its algorithm id, not the whole certificate.
SHA-256 over exactly those bytes.
Base64 the digest — that is the sha256/… string in your pin list.
Compare against the pins compiled into the app. Any match passes; no match drops the connection.
The app never discovers the key — you put it there, read once from the server you control.
That is the whole trust anchor: the pin is believed because it shipped with the app, not because the network said so.
TLS does the other half: the server must sign the handshake with the matching private key, so presenting a certificate is not enough.
A copy of your certificate is therefore useless to an attacker. The private key never leaves the server.
Most libraries test every certificate in the chain, so a pin may name the leaf key or its issuer.

blocks.text: But the public key is public — why can it not be copied?

items: It can. Anyone may download your certificate and read the key out of it.
The copy is useless: TLS makes the server sign the handshake with the private key, which never leaves the server.
So an attacker presenting your certificate is dropped at the signature, before any data moves — the pin is never even reached.
Using their own key pair fails the other way round: a valid handshake, the wrong pin, connection dropped.
The pin says which key to expect; TLS proves the peer is holding it. Neither half is enough on its own.

body: Hashing the whole certificate instead of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo is the classic mistake: the digest then changes at every renewal, even when the key did not.

sections.title: The handshake, end to end
sections.summary: Where the pin check sits in a real TLS 1.3 exchange.

blocks.caption: TLS 1.3. In 1.2 the messages differ, but the pin check sits in the same place.

items.label: 1. ClientHello
items.detail: App → server: versions, ciphers, its key share, the hostname in SNI
explain: The first message on the connection, sent in the clear: nothing is encrypted yet, so anyone on the path reads all of it.
'Versions' is the list of TLS versions the app can speak, say 1.3 and 1.2. The server picks the highest both sides know.
A cipher suite is the named recipe for the session: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 means AES-128 in GCM mode for the data and SHA-256 for the hashing. The client sends the ones it supports.

A key share is a temporary public key generated for this session only, usually X25519. Temporary is the point — it is thrown away afterwards, so a key stolen next year cannot decrypt today's recording.
SNI (Server Name Indication) carries the hostname in plaintext, because one IP address may serve thousands of sites. It is also the field a proxy reads to know which name to forge.

items.label: 2. ServerHello
items.detail: Server → app: chosen cipher and the server key share
explain: The server answers with exactly one of each: one version, one cipher suite, one key share — chosen out of the lists it was offered.
For example TLS 1.3 with TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and a key share over X25519. Both sides are now committed to that recipe.
Everything after this message is encrypted with keys derived from the two key shares, the certificate in message 4 included.
There is still no proof of identity here. A proxy answers this message exactly the way your server does; identity only arrives in message 5.

items.label: 3. Shared secret
items.detail: Both sides derive it from the two key shares. Everything below is encrypted
explain: Diffie–Hellman: each side combines its own private value with the other side's public key share, and both land on the same secret without it ever crossing the wire.
So an eavesdropper who captured every single byte still cannot compute it, because neither private half was ever sent.
From that secret, both derive the real session keys — one per direction — and the rest of the handshake is already encrypted.
This is forward secrecy: the key pair in cert_A is used for signing only, never to encrypt the session, so stealing priv_key_A later does not unlock a recording made today.

items.label: 4. Certificate
items.detail: Server → app: the leaf certificate and its intermediates
explain: The server sends cert_A and the intermediates above it — the leaf holding pub_key_A, then R3. The root is not sent, because the device already has it.
The contents are public information; they are encrypted here only so an eavesdropper cannot see which site you are visiting.
This is the exact message pinning inspects. The hash the app compares is taken from the SPKI field of the leaf certificate in this message.
Note how much has been proved at this point: nothing. Anyone can download cert_A from your public server, so this message is worth nothing without the next one.

items.label: 5. CertificateVerify
items.detail: Server signs the transcript with its private key — the step a copied certificate cannot fake
explain: The server signs a hash of the entire handshake so far — every byte of every message — using priv_key_A, the private half of the key inside cert_A.
The client verifies that signature with pub_key_A, taken from the certificate it received a moment ago. A peer without the private half cannot produce it.
This is why copying cert_A off a public website gets an attacker nowhere: no priv_key_A, no valid CertificateVerify, no connection.
And it is why pinning a key means something. The pin says 'this exact key'; CertificateVerify says 'and I hold its private half'.

items.label: 6. Finished
items.detail: A MAC over the whole transcript, proving both sides derived the same keys
explain: Each side sends a MAC — a keyed hash — computed over the whole transcript of the handshake, with keys derived from the shared secret.
If anything on the path altered an earlier message, say deleting TLS 1.3 from the client's list to force a weaker version, the two transcripts differ and this check fails.
That is downgrade protection: the negotiation cannot be rewritten in flight without both sides noticing right here.
Once Finished is exchanged, the connection is established and application data may start flowing.

items.label: 7a. Chain
items.detail: Each certificate signed by the next, up to a root the device already trusts
explain: Verification walks upward: cert_A must be signed by R3's key, R3 by the root's key, and that root must already sit in the device's trust store.
The trust store is the fixed list shipped with the OS, plus whatever a configuration profile or an MDM added later — which is exactly how a corporate or attacker CA gets in.
The most common real failure here is a missing intermediate: the server never sent R3, so a device that has not cached it cannot complete the chain, while other devices work fine.
Passing this step says only that some trusted CA vouched for some key. It does not say which key, and that gap is the whole reason pinning exists.

items.label: 7b. Hostname
items.detail: The certificate must list the domain you asked for in its SAN field
explain: The client checks that api.example.com appears in the certificate's SAN list — Subject Alternative Name, which can hold several names and wildcards such as *.example.com.
The old Common Name field is ignored by iOS and Android today, so a certificate carrying only a CN fails on any modern device.
Without this check, a certificate legitimately issued for evil.example could be used to answer for your domain — the CA did nothing wrong, the client just failed to look.
The name checked is the one from the URL, not the one in SNI, so an attacker cannot slip through by lying in the hello.

items.label: 7c. Validity
items.detail: Inside its dates, and not on a revocation list the device can reach
explain: notBefore and notAfter are compared against the device clock. Public certificates now last 90 days or less, so this is a live constraint rather than a formality.
A phone with the wrong date fails every HTTPS connection at once — the classic 'nothing works since the battery died' bug.
Revocation is the weak half: OCSP or a CRL says whether a certificate was cancelled early, but the check is often unreachable and most clients continue anyway.
Pinning does not depend on revocation, which is part of its value: a compromised key stops working the moment you stop pinning it, not when a CA gets round to it.

items.label: 8. Pin check
items.detail: SPKI → SHA-256 → base64, compared with the pins in the app
explain: The app's own step, run after the OS is satisfied: didReceiveChallenge in URLSession, CertificatePinner in OkHttp, badCertificateCallback or a Dio adapter in Flutter.
It takes the leaf from message 4, extracts SPKI, hashes it to sha256/…, and compares against the pins compiled into the build: pin_A, and ideally pin_B as the spare.
Run it in addition to the OS checks, never instead of them — replacing them means accepting an expired certificate, or the wrong hostname, as long as the key matches.
Compare against a list and accept the first match, so the day the server moves to key_B nothing in the app has to change.

items.label: All pass
items.detail: Client Finished, then the first request is sent
explain: The client sends its own Finished and the handshake is complete — one round trip, in the common TLS 1.3 case.
Only now does the first application byte leave the device: GET /v1/profile, with its Authorization header attached.
The session is then reused for the rest of the connection, so the pin is checked once per connection rather than once per request.

items.label: Any fails
items.detail: Alert, connection closed, nothing sent
explain: The client sends a TLS alert — bad_certificate, certificate_expired or unknown_ca — and closes the socket immediately.
In the app it surfaces as a transport error: -1202 on iOS, SSLPeerUnverifiedException on Android, HandshakeException in Dart.
No part of the request was written, so a failed check costs a retry and never a leaked token, cookie or body.
Log which of the four checks failed and what pin was presented. Without that line, a rotation mistake and a real attack look identical in your crash reports.

items: Steps 4 to 8 are already encrypted; an observer sees only the ClientHello and the hostname in SNI.
Step 5 is what makes a stolen copy of your certificate useless — signing needs the private key.
Step 8 is the only part the library adds. Steps 7a to 7c happen with or without pinning.
The pin is checked before the first byte of your request leaves, not after a reply comes back.

sections.title: Always ship a backup pin
sections.summary: This is the section that decides whether pinning ever bricks your app.

blocks.caption: The app already trusts the next key before the server switches to it.

items.label: Pin A
items.detail: The hash of the key the server is actually serving today
explain: pin_A is SHA-256(SPKI(pub_key_A)): the hash of the key inside the certificate your server is serving right now.
Renewing that certificate — cert_A becomes cert_A2 next quarter — leaves pin_A untouched, as long as the CSR reuses the same key pair.
That has to be a deliberate decision on the server side: certbot and most ACME clients generate a fresh key on every renewal unless you tell them not to.
If a renewal quietly rotates the key while pin_A is the only pin in the app, every installed copy stops working the minute the new certificate goes live.

items.label: Pin B
items.detail: The hash of a key you generated early and locked away, not in use yet
explain: Generate key_B now, keep it offline — a password manager, an HSM, a sealed envelope — and pin its hash even though no certificate uses it yet.
You do not need a certificate to compute it: openssl pkey -in key_B.pem -pubout -outform der | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl enc -base64.
This is the difference between an incident you fix on the server in an hour, and one that needs an emergency release plus a week of review.
Store key_B somewhere priv_key_A is not, or one break takes both halves of the plan at the same time.

items.label: Both ship in the release
items.detail: The app accepts either, so it is ready for the switch months before it happens
explain: The app's pin set is [pin_A, pin_B] and the check passes if either matches — the normal behaviour of NSPinnedDomains and CertificatePinner alike.
Users update when they feel like it, so the spare has to be in the field long before the switch. Assume months, not days.
Shipping pin_B leaks nothing: a pin is a hash of a public key, and the private half of key_B is still in your safe.

items.label: Server moves to key B
items.detail: Installed apps keep working, because pin B was already in their list
explain: The switch is server-side only: issue a certificate for key_B, deploy it, and every installed app that holds pin_B carries on through the change.
No release, no review queue, no message to users — which is the entire reason the spare was shipped months earlier.
Do it deliberately once in a while even without an incident: a rotation path you have never exercised is a rotation path you do not know works.

items.label: Next release adds pin C
items.detail: Pin C replaces the one just retired, so there is always a spare in hand
explain: After the switch, key_B is the live one and pin_A points at a retired key, so the next release ships [pin_B, pin_C] with key_C generated and locked away.
Keep the retired pin for one more release while old versions drain out of the field, then drop it.
The invariant to hold: at every moment, every installed version accepts the key in use plus exactly one key that is not in use yet.

items: A single pin means the day the key changes, every installed app stops working.
Users on old versions cannot be fixed by a server change — only by a store update.
Generate the backup key now and keep it offline; a pin for a key you own is useless if it is lost with the server.
Pin only your own API. Third-party SDKs rotate on their schedule, not yours.

sections.title: Android
sections.summary: Config for the whole app, or OkHttp for one client.

blocks.caption: res/xml/network_security_config.xml — expiration disables the pin instead of killing the app

body: Point android:networkSecurityConfig at the file in the manifest, or nothing is enforced.

items: By hand it is a URLSessionDelegate that hashes the SPKI of the leaf and compares.
Never call completionHandler(.useCredential, …) without comparing — that turns pinning off.
TrustKit also reports failures, which is how you find a bad rollout early.

body: badCertificateCallback is not pinning. It only runs after validation already failed, and returning true there weakens TLS instead of strengthening it.

blocks.caption: Trust only your own CA, nothing the device trusts

items: This pins the CA, so renewing the leaf under the same CA keeps working.
For SPKI pinning use a package that hashes the key, and ship two hashes.
Bundle the .pem as an asset; do not fetch it over the network you are protecting.

sections.title: Prove it works
sections.summary: A pin you never tested is a pin you do not have.

items: Run mitmproxy and install its CA on the device or simulator.
Open the app without pinning: requests appear in the proxy.
Turn pinning on and repeat: the calls must fail, not merely look empty.
Change one pin to a wrong value and confirm the app fails closed.
Test on a release build. Debug builds often trust user CAs and hide the result.
Add a test that fails if the pin list is empty, so a bad merge cannot silently disable it.

rows: The key changes and every installed app is dead until users update.
Anyone who buys a certificate from that CA passes the check.
Analytics or payments break on their rotation schedule, not yours.
No expiry and no kill switch
A bad pin can only be fixed by a store release, which takes days.
